title: 1. How Ansible Works
text:
The Lemonade Stand has two web servers, web1 and web2. Both need the same nginx config, the same menu page and the same app settings. Today you log in to each one with SSH and type the commands by hand.
That goes wrong in three ways:

Drift. You forget one command on web2. Now the two servers are different, and nobody notices until customers on web2 see the old prices.
No record. Six months later nobody remembers what was typed.
It does not scale. Two servers take ten minutes. Twenty servers take all afternoon.

We want to write the steps down once, run them on every server, and run them again safely whenever we like.

title: 1. How Ansible Works
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipA walkie-talkie and a checklist



In Ursula K. Le Guin’s 1966 science-fiction novel Rocannon’s World, an ansible is a machine that sends messages instantly to anyone, anywhere in the galaxy. The software is named after it. You stand in one place and talk to all your servers at once.
Now imagine you are the captain of a lemonade stand with two helpers. You don’t tell them “pour one cup of sugar”. If you said that every time, you would end up with far too much sugar. Instead you hand each helper a checklist that says what things should look like:

“The jug has sugar in it.”
“The sign says Lemonade $2.50.”

A helper checks each line. If it is already true, they do nothing. If it is not true, they fix it. You can read the checklist to them a hundred times and the lemonade never gets too sweet.
Ansible works the same way. Your laptop is the captain, the servers are the helpers, and a playbook is the checklist.

title: 1. How Ansible Works
text:
The concept, precisely

The pieces



Piece
What it is
Lemonade Stand example




Control node
The machine where Ansible is installed and where you type commands.
Your laptop.


Managed node (host)
A machine Ansible configures. Ansible does not need to be installed on it.
web1, web2, db1.


Inventory
A file that lists the managed nodes and puts them into groups.
inventory.yml: groups web, db, prod.


Module
A small program that does one job, such as copy a file or install a package.
ansible.builtin.template renders the nginx config.


Task
One call to one module, with arguments.
“Render the nginx config”.


Play
A list of tasks aimed at a group of hosts.
“Configure the web servers” for hosts: web.


Playbook
A YAML file with one or more plays.
site.yml.


Role
A folder that packages tasks, templates and defaults for reuse.
roles/lemonade_web/.





What happens when a task runs
Ansible is agentless: nothing runs on the servers between Ansible runs. For each task and each host, Ansible:

connects to the host, usually over SSH;
copies the module’s code to a temporary folder on the host;
runs it with the host’s Python and gets back a JSON result such as {"changed": true};
deletes the temporary folder;
prints the result: ok, changed, failed, skipped or unreachable.

control node                                  managed node web1
┌─────────────────────┐   1. ssh             ┌──────────────────────┐
│ ansible-playbook    │ ───────────────────► │ sshd                 │
│ reads site.yml      │   2. copy module     │ ~/.ansible/tmp/...   │
│                     │ ───────────────────► │ 3. python3 module    │
│ prints "changed"    │ ◄─────────────────── │    returns JSON      │
└─────────────────────┘   4. delete tmp      └──────────────────────┘
This is a push model. The control node decides when to change things and pushes the work out. Other tools, such as Puppet or Chef, normally run an agent on every server that pulls its configuration on a timer. Ansible can pull too, with ansible-pull (lesson 12), but push is the normal way.


Desired state and idempotency
Most modules are declarative. You describe the end result, not the steps:
- name: Make sure the site folder exists
  ansible.builtin.file:
    path: /srv/lemonade/site
    state: directory      # "should be a directory", not "run mkdir"
The module first checks the current state. Then it acts only if the state is wrong:



Current state on the host
What the module does
Result shown




Folder is missing
Creates it
changed


Folder already exists
Nothing
ok


A file with that name exists
Cannot fix this safely
failed



An operation is idempotent when doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Idempotency makes it safe to run a playbook again. When you are not sure whether a server is correct, run the playbook. It fixes only what has drifted.
The command and shell modules are the exception. Ansible cannot know what an arbitrary shell command does, so it runs the command every time and reports changed every time. Lesson 5 shows how to make them behave.


What you need







Machine
Requirement (ansible-core 2.21)




Control node
Linux, macOS or Windows with WSL; Python 3.12 or newer.


Managed node (Linux)
An SSH server, a user you can log in as, and Python 3.9 or newer.


Managed node (Windows)
WinRM or SSH plus PowerShell, using the ansible.windows collection.

title: 1. How Ansible Works
text:
Every install and first-run command









Command
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




pipx install ansible-core
Installs only the engine and the ansible.builtin modules into an isolated environment.
Recommended for learning. Add collections later as you need them.
pipx install ansible-core


pipx install --include-deps ansible
Installs the “batteries included” package: ansible-core plus about 90 community collections.
Bigger download. --include-deps is needed so pipx exposes the ansible-* commands.
pipx install --include-deps ansible


python3 -m pip install --user ansible
Installs with pip for the current user.
Use a virtual environment to avoid clashing with system packages.
python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install ansible-core


brew install ansible
Installs the full package on macOS with Homebrew.
Homebrew upgrades Ansible together with your other formulae.
brew install ansible


ansible --version
Prints the version, the config file in use, and the Python it runs on.
Run it first when something behaves oddly. The config file line tells you which ansible.cfg won.
ansible --version


ansible localhost -m ansible.builtin.ping
Runs the ping module on your own machine.
ping does not send network pings. It checks that Ansible can log in and run Python.
see below

title: 1. How Ansible Works
text:
Worked example: your first run
From any folder with no inventory, Ansible still knows one host, the implicit localhost:
ansible localhost -m ansible.builtin.ping
[WARNING]: No inventory was parsed, only implicit localhost is available
localhost | SUCCESS => {
    "changed": false,
    "ping": "pong"
}
SUCCESS and "ping": "pong" mean Ansible ran Python on the target and got an answer. "changed": false means nothing on the machine was modified.
Now run the lab playbook. From devops/ansible/examples/:
ansible-playbook site.yml
First run (trimmed to the lines that matter):
TASK [lemonade_web : Render the nginx config] **********************************
changed: [web1]
changed: [web2]

RUNNING HANDLER [lemonade_web : Reload nginx] **********************************
ok: [web1] =>
    msg: nginx reloaded on web1

PLAY RECAP *********************************************************************
db1    : ok=2    changed=2    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0
web1   : ok=4    changed=3    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0
web2   : ok=4    changed=3    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0
Second run of exactly the same command:
PLAY RECAP *********************************************************************
db1    : ok=2    changed=0    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0
web1   : ok=3    changed=0    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0
web2   : ok=3    changed=0    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0
What changed between the runs:

Every task now reports ok, because the files already look the way the playbook describes.
ok dropped from 4 to 3 on the web hosts. The handler “Reload nginx” did not run, because no task changed anything. Handlers are covered in lesson 8.
changed=0 everywhere. That is the proof that the playbook is idempotent.

The result on “web1’s disk”, /tmp/lemonade-lab/web1/nginx/lemonade.conf:
# Ansible managed
worker_processes 4;
server {
    listen 80;
    location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080; }
}

title: 1. How Ansible Works
text:
Rules and conventions

Describe the state, not the steps. Prefer state: present, state: directory and state: started over shell commands.
Use fully qualified module names (FQCN), such as ansible.builtin.copy rather than copy. The long name says exactly which collection the module comes from.
Give every task a name that reads like a line on a checklist: “Render the menu page”.
Run twice to test. A good playbook reports changed=0 on its second run.
Keep everything in Git: inventory, playbooks, roles and variables. The repository becomes the record of how your servers are built.
Use --check --diff before risky changes (lesson 4).

title: 1. How Ansible Works
text:
Common mistakes



Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Installing Ansible on the servers
Nothing breaks, but it is unnecessary work.
Install it only on the control node. Managed nodes need SSH and Python.


Using shell: mkdir -p /srv/lemonade
The task reports changed on every run, and handlers fire every time.
Use ansible.builtin.file with state: directory.


Thinking ping sends ICMP packets
ping fails even though ping 192.0.2.11 in a terminal works.
ansible.builtin.ping needs SSH login and Python. Check the user, the SSH key and the Python path.


Managed node has no Python
/usr/bin/python3: not found
Install Python first, for example with the raw module (lesson 5).


Running from the wrong folder
Ansible says “No inventory was parsed”.
Run from the folder that holds ansible.cfg, or pass -i inventory.yml.

title: 1. How Ansible Works
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
Model one server as a state \(s\): everything Ansible could check, such as which files exist and what they contain. A task is a function that turns one state into another.
\[
f(f(s)) = f(s) \quad \text{for every state } s \in S
\]
where:

\(S\) is the set of all possible states of a server (every combination of files, packages and services);
\(s\) is one particular state, for example “web1 with no nginx config yet”;
\(f : S \to S\) is a task, such as “the file lemonade.conf has this content”;
\(f(s)\) is the state after running the task once, and \(f(f(s))\) the state after running it twice.

The equation says that the second run changes nothing. A function with this property is called idempotent.
Example. Let \(f\) be the task “the folder /tmp/lemonade-lab/web1/nginx exists”.

Start state \(s_0\): the folder does not exist.
After one run, \(f(s_0) = s_1\), where \(s_1\) is “the folder exists”. Ansible reports changed.
After a second run, \(f(s_1) = s_1\), because the folder already exists. Ansible reports ok.
So \(f(f(s_0)) = f(s_1) = s_1 = f(s_0)\). The equation holds.

A whole playbook run on one host can be summarised by the number of tasks that reported changed:
\[
C_k = \sum_{h \in H} c_{h,k}
\]
where:

\(H\) is the set of hosts in the run, here \(H = \lbrace \texttt{web1}, \texttt{web2}, \texttt{db1} \rbrace\);
\(k\) is the run number: \(k = 1\) for the first run and \(k = 2\) for the second;
\(c_{h,k}\) is the changed= number that PLAY RECAP prints for host \(h\) in run \(k\);
\(C_k\) is the total number of changes in run \(k\).

Example, using the real output above:

First run: \(C_1 = c_{\texttt{db1},1} + c_{\texttt{web1},1} + c_{\texttt{web2},1} = 2 + 3 + 3 = 8\).
Second run: \(C_2 = 0 + 0 + 0 = 0\).

\(C_2 = 0\) is the practical test of idempotency. If \(C_2 > 0\) and nobody changed the servers between the runs, some task is not idempotent and should be fixed.

title: 8. Conditionals, Loops and Handlers
text:
A real Lemonade deploy is not a straight line:

Install apt packages only on Debian servers, and dnf packages only on Fedora servers. (Conditionals)
Create the same kind of folder three times without writing three tasks. (Loops)
After starting the app, wait until it answers, but give up after a while. (Retries)
Reload nginx after a config change, but only once, and only if something really changed. (Handlers)
If the deploy fails, roll back and always clean up. (Blocks)

title: 8. Conditionals, Loops and Handlers
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipMum’s morning instructions




“If it’s raining, take your umbrella.” That is when.
“Give each friend at your party one balloon.” That is loop.
“Knock on Grandma’s door. If she doesn’t answer, wait a minute and knock again. Try five times, then come home.” That is until / retries / delay.
“If you changed anything in the kitchen, tell me. I’ll do the washing-up once, at the end.” That is a handler. Ten changes still mean one washing-up.
“Try to bake the cake. If it burns, we’ll buy one. Either way, clean the kitchen.” That is block / rescue / always.

title: 8. Conditionals, Loops and Handlers
text:
Conditionals: when
when takes a bare Jinja expression, without { }. If it is false, the task is skipped. Since ansible-core 2.19, the result must be a real boolean, not a string or a number.









Form
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




Comparison
Runs if the comparison is true.
==, !=, <, >, <=, >=
when: lemonade_app_port != 80


Fact
Branch on the OS or hardware.
Use ansible_facts[...].
when: ansible_facts['os_family'] == 'Debian'


List of conditions
Runs only if all are true (AND).
One condition per line reads well.
when: [a > 1, b == 2]


and, or, not
Combine conditions.
Use brackets with or.
when: (x == 1) or (y == 2)


Test
Ask a yes/no question.

when: lemonade_menu is defined


Registered result
React to an earlier task.

when: nginx_conf is changed


Boolean variable
Runs if the variable is true.
From -e, convert with \| bool.
when: lemonade_enable_tls \| bool


Membership
Is this host in a group?

when: inventory_hostname in groups['web']

title: 8. Conditionals, Loops and Handlers
text:
Loops









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




loop
Runs the task once per item; the item is item.
A list, or an expression that gives a list.
loop: [nginx, site]


loop over dictionaries
Each item is a dictionary.
Read fields as item.name.
loop: "{{ lemonade_menu }}"


loop over a dictionary
Turn it into a list first.

loop: "{{ ports \| dict2items }}"


loop_control.label
What to print for each item.
Keeps output short for big dictionaries.
label: "{{ item.name }}"


loop_control.loop_var
Renames item.
Required in nested loops (a loop inside an included file).
loop_var: drink


loop_control.index_var
Puts the item’s index (0, 1, 2…) in a variable.

index_var: idx


loop_control.pause
Seconds to wait between items.

pause: 2


loop_control.extended
Adds ansible_loop.index, .first, .last, .length.

extended: true


loop_control.break_when
Stops the loop early when a condition is true.

break_when: [result is failed]



Older playbooks use with_* keywords. They still work, but loop is the modern form:







Legacy
Modern equivalent




with_items: "{{ list }}"
loop: "{{ list \| flatten(levels=1) }}"


with_list: "{{ list }}"
loop: "{{ list }}"


with_dict: "{{ d }}"
loop: "{{ d \| dict2items }}"


with_fileglob: "*.j2"
loop: "{{ query('ansible.builtin.fileglob', '*.j2') }}"


with_sequence: start=1 end=3
loop: "{{ range(1, 4) \| list }}"


with_together: [a, b]
loop: "{{ a \| zip(b) \| list }}"


with_nested: [a, b]
loop: "{{ a \| product(b) \| list }}"

title: 8. Conditionals, Loops and Handlers
text:
Retrying: until









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




until
Repeats the task until this condition is true.
Needs register to test the result.
until: health.status == 200


retries
How many extra tries after the first one.
Default 3 when until is set.
retries: 10


delay
Seconds to wait between tries.
Default 5.
delay: 3


attempts
Added to the registered result.

health.attempts

title: 8. Conditionals, Loops and Handlers
text:
Handlers









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




handlers:
A list of tasks that run only when notified.
In a play, or in a role’s handlers/main.yml.
handlers: [...]


notify
Notifies a handler if this task reported changed.
Use the handler’s exact name, or a list of names.
notify: Reload nginx


listen
Gives a handler a topic that tasks can notify.
Lets several handlers react to one event.
listen: web config changed


meta: flush_handlers
Runs notified handlers now, not at the end.
When later tasks need the restarted service.
ansible.builtin.meta: flush_handlers


--force-handlers
Runs notified handlers even after a failure.

ansible-playbook site.yml --force-handlers



Handler rules:

A notified handler runs once, at the end of the section (pre_tasks, roles/tasks, post_tasks), however many tasks notified it.
Handlers run in the order they are defined, not the order they were notified.
A handler is not run for a host where a later task failed, unless you force it.

title: 8. Conditionals, Loops and Handlers
text:
Deciding the result yourself









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




changed_when
Sets when the task counts as changed.
false for read-only commands.
changed_when: false


failed_when
Sets when the task counts as failed.
Lets you accept some non-zero exit codes.
failed_when: result.rc not in [0, 1]


ignore_errors
Continue after a failure.
Shows as ignored in the recap. Prefer failed_when.
ignore_errors: true


ignore_unreachable
Continue after a connection failure.

ignore_unreachable: true

text:
Blocks









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




block
Groups tasks. Keywords on the block (when, become, tags) apply to all of them.

block: [...]


rescue
Runs only if a task in block failed.
The host counts as rescued, not failed.
rescue: [...]


always
Runs whether or not block failed.
For cleanup.
always: [...]


ansible_failed_task
The task that failed, inside rescue.

{ ansible_failed_task.name }


ansible_failed_result
That task’s result.

{ ansible_failed_result.msg }

title: 8. Conditionals, Loops and Handlers
text:
Worked examples
Each block below was run with ansible-core 2.21. The output is trimmed to the lines that prove the point.
A loop with a label and an index:
- name: Print each drink
  ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg: "{{ idx + 1 }}. {{ drink.name }} costs {{ drink.price }}"
  loop: "{{ lemonade_menu }}"
  loop_control: { loop_var: drink, index_var: idx, label: "{{ drink.name }}" }
ok: [localhost] => (item=Classic Lemonade) =>
    msg: 1. Classic Lemonade costs 2.5
ok: [localhost] => (item=Pink Lemonade) =>
    msg: 2. Pink Lemonade costs 3.0
Retry until the app is up. Here a small web server started about 1.5 seconds after the task, so the second try succeeded:
- name: Wait for the Lemonade app
  ansible.builtin.uri: { url: "http://127.0.0.1:8080/health" }
  register: health
  until: health.status == 200
  retries: 5
  delay: 1
FAILED - RETRYING: [localhost]: Wait for the Lemonade app (4 retries left).
ok: [localhost]
Two changes, one handler run. In the lab role, both templates notify Reload nginx. On the first run both changed, and the handler still ran once per host:
TASK [lemonade_web : Render the nginx config] ****
changed: [web1]
TASK [lemonade_web : Render the menu page] *******
changed: [web1]
RUNNING HANDLER [lemonade_web : Reload nginx] ****
ok: [web1] =>
    msg: nginx reloaded on web1
Rescue and clean up:
- block:
    - name: Deploy step that fails
      ansible.builtin.command: "false"
  rescue:
    - ansible.builtin.debug: { msg: "rolling back: {{ ansible_failed_task.name }} failed" }
  always:
    - ansible.builtin.debug: { msg: "cleanup done" }
fatal: [localhost]: FAILED! => ... rc: 1
ok: [localhost] =>
    msg: 'rolling back: Deploy step that fails failed'
ok: [localhost] =>
    msg: cleanup done
localhost : ok=2    changed=0    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=1    ignored=0
The recap says failed=0, rescued=1. The failure was handled.
Accept a harmless exit code. grep -c exits with 1 when it finds nothing:
- ansible.builtin.command: grep -c Mango /srv/lemonade/menu.txt
  register: mango
  failed_when: mango.rc not in [0, 1]
  changed_when: false

title: 8. Conditionals, Loops and Handlers
text:
Rules and conventions

No { } in when, until, changed_when or failed_when. They are already expressions.
Convert -e values with | bool. -e lemonade_enable_tls=false passes the string "false".
Use handlers for restarts and reloads, never plain tasks with state: restarted.
Name handlers clearly, such as “Reload nginx”, and notify them by that exact name.
Use loop_var whenever a loop runs inside another loop.
Prefer failed_when over ignore_errors. Say which failures are fine instead of hiding all of them.
Always set retries and delay with until, so the reader sees the time limit.

title: 8. Conditionals, Loops and Handlers
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




-e use_tls=false with when: use_tls
Conditional result (True) was derived from value of type 'str' ... Conditionals must have a boolean result.
when: use_tls \| bool, or pass JSON: -e '{"use_tls": false}'.


notify: reload nginx (wrong case)
The requested handler 'reload nginx' was not found in either the main handlers list nor in the listening handlers list
Match the handler’s name exactly.


Expecting a handler to run mid-play
A later task fails because nginx still has the old config.
Add - ansible.builtin.meta: flush_handlers.


until without register
The condition reads an undefined variable.
register: health, then until: health.status == 200.


ignore_errors: true on a real failure
failed=0, but the server is broken.
Remove it; use failed_when for specific cases.

title: 8. Conditionals, Loops and Handlers
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
Retries. With until, a task runs at most \(r + 1\) times and waits between runs:
\[
N_{\max} = r + 1, \qquad W_{\max} = r \cdot d
\]
where:

\(r\) is retries, the number of extra tries (\(r \ge 0\); default 3);
\(d\) is delay, the wait between tries in seconds (default 5);
\(N_{\max}\) is the largest number of times the task runs;
\(W_{\max}\) is the longest total waiting time in seconds, not counting the time the task itself takes.

Example 1, the health check above: \(r = 5\) and \(d = 1\), so \(N_{\max} = 5 + 1 = 6\) runs and \(W_{\max} = 5 \cdot 1 = 5\) s. It succeeded on try \(k = 2\), so it waited \((k - 1) \cdot d = 1 \cdot 1 = 1\) s.
Example 2, defaults: \(r = 3\) and \(d = 5\) give \(N_{\max} = 4\) runs and \(W_{\max} = 15\) s. If the app needs 30 s to start, the defaults are too short. Choose \(r\) and \(d\) so that \(r \cdot d \ge 30\), for example \(r = 10\) and \(d = 3\).
Handlers. Let task \(i\) notify handler \(H\). A handler runs at most once per section:
\[
\operatorname{runs}(H) =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } \sum_{i} n_i \ge 1 \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\qquad
n_i =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if task } i \text{ notifies } H \text{ and reported changed} \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]
where the sum runs over every task in the section, and \(\operatorname{runs}(H)\) is how many times \(H\) runs on that host.
Example. First run of site.yml on web1: both templates changed, so \(n_1 + n_2 = 1 + 1 = 2 \ge 1\), and “Reload nginx” runs once. Second run: nothing changed, so \(n_1 + n_2 = 0 + 0 = 0\), and the handler runs zero times. That is why the second run’s ok count dropped from 4 to 3 in lesson 1.
Loops. A looped task runs once per item, on each host:
\[
E = \lvert L \rvert \cdot \lvert H \rvert
\]
where \(\lvert L \rvert\) is the number of items in the loop list, \(\lvert H \rvert\) is the number of hosts, and \(E\) is the number of module executions.
Example. “Create the nginx and site folders” loops over \(L\) = [nginx, site] on \(H\) = {web1, web2}: \(E = 2 \cdot 2 = 4\) executions. That matches the four changed: [...] => (item=...) lines of the first run.

title: 8. Conditionals, Loops and Handlers

title: 9. Roles and Collections
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipLEGO sets



A LEGO set comes in a box. Inside there is everything for one model: the pieces, the instruction booklet, and a sticker sheet with suggested colours. You can build the same set at home and at Grandma’s house, and it comes out the same. If you want a red car instead of a blue one, you choose your own stickers. The instructions stay the same.
A role is one LEGO set. Tasks are the instructions, templates and files are the pieces, and defaults is the sticker sheet you are allowed to change.
A collection is a whole LEGO theme, like the “City” range: many sets, plus special pieces (modules) that you can’t get anywhere else. Ansible Galaxy is the toy shop.

title: 9. Roles and Collections
text:
The concept, precisely

A role is a folder with a fixed layout. Ansible knows where to look inside it, so you write roles: [lemonade_web] and it finds the tasks, handlers, templates and defaults by itself.
A collection is a package of modules, plugins and roles, published under a name namespace.collection such as community.general. You install it with ansible-galaxy.
A fully qualified collection name (FQCN) points at one item inside a collection: community.general.ufw.


The role folder convention
ansible-galaxy role init lemonade_db creates this skeleton (real output, ansible-core 2.21):
lemonade_db/
├── README.md
├── defaults/main.yml     # tunable variables (lowest precedence)
├── files/                # static files for copy / script / unarchive
├── handlers/main.yml     # handlers
├── meta/main.yml         # author, licence, dependencies
├── tasks/main.yml        # the entry point: tasks run in order
├── templates/            # .j2 files for template
├── tests/                # inventory + test.yml to try the role
└── vars/main.yml         # internal constants (high precedence)









Folder or file
What it holds
Rule / convention
Example




tasks/main.yml
The role’s tasks.
Required. Split long roles with include_tasks.
- name: Render the nginx config


handlers/main.yml
The role’s handlers.
Other roles in the same play can notify them.
- name: Reload nginx


defaults/main.yml
Every variable a user may change.
Precedence level 2: anything overrides it. Prefix names with the role name.
lemonade_app_port: 8080


vars/main.yml
Values users should not change.
Level 15: overrides inventory.
lemonade_folders: [nginx, site]


templates/
Jinja2 files.
template: src: nginx.conf.j2 finds them here.
templates/nginx.conf.j2


files/
Static files.
copy: src: logo.png finds them here.
files/logo.png


meta/main.yml
Metadata and dependencies.
dependencies: run before this role.
dependencies: [common]


meta/argument_specs.yml
Types of the role’s inputs.
Checked automatically before tasks/main.yml.
see below


library/
Custom modules for this role.

library/lemonade_check.py


README.md
How to use the role.
Document every default.

text:
Every way to use a role









Way
When Ansible processes it
Rule / convention
Example




roles: in a play
Static, when the playbook is read. Runs before tasks:.
The classic form.
roles: [lemonade_web]


roles: with parameters
Static.
Parameters are precedence level 20.
roles: [{ role: lemonade_web, lemonade_app_port: 9090 }]


import_role
Static, at the place you write it in tasks:.
when and tags are copied onto every task inside. Tasks show in --list-tasks.
ansible.builtin.import_role: { name: lemonade_web }


include_role
Dynamic, only when the task is reached.
Can be looped and decided at run time. Inner tasks are hidden from --list-tasks.
ansible.builtin.include_role: { name: "{{ app_role }}" }



The same split exists for plain task files:









Keyword
Kind
Use it when
Example




import_tasks
Static
The file name is fixed and you want --list-tasks and --start-at-task to see the tasks.
ansible.builtin.import_tasks: install.yml


include_tasks
Dynamic
The file name comes from a variable, or you loop over it.
ansible.builtin.include_tasks: "{{ ansible_facts['os_family'] }}.yml"



Real --list-tasks output for one import_role and one include_role of the same small role:
    tasks:
      greet : Validating arguments against arg spec 'main' - Say hello. TAGS: [always]
      ansible.builtin.debug TAGS: []
      ansible.builtin.include_role  TAGS: []
The imported role’s tasks are listed. The included role is one opaque task until it runs.

Run once, unless the parameters differ
Within one play, a role listed twice with the same parameters runs only once. To run it again, give it different parameters, or set allow_duplicates: true in its meta/main.yml.


Argument specs
meta/argument_specs.yml declares the role’s inputs. Ansible adds a validation task at the start of the role.
argument_specs:
  main:
    short_description: Configure a Lemonade web server.
    options:
      lemonade_app_port: { type: int, required: true }
      lemonade_menu: { type: list, elements: dict }
Passing -e lemonade_app_port=abc now fails early, with a clear message, before any file is touched:
Validation of arguments failed:
argument 'lemonade_app_port' is of type str and we were unable to convert to int

Collections









Command or file
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




ansible-galaxy collection install NAME
Installs a collection from Galaxy.
Into ~/.ansible/collections by default.
ansible-galaxy collection install community.general


… install NAME:VERSION
Installs a specific version or range.
Quote ranges in the shell.
ansible-galaxy collection install 'community.general:>=9.0.0,<10.0.0'


… install -r requirements.yml
Installs everything in a requirements file.
Commit this file; run it in CI.

… install -p DIR
Installs into a project folder.
Pair with collections_path in ansible.cfg.
-p ./collections


ansible-galaxy collection list
Shows installed collections and versions.

ansible-galaxy collection list community.general


ansible-galaxy role install NAME
Installs a standalone role from Galaxy.
Older style; many roles now live in collections.
ansible-galaxy role install geerlingguy.nginx


collections: play keyword
Lets you write short module names.
Prefer the FQCN instead; it is clearer.
collections: [community.general]

collections:
  - name: ansible.posix
    version: ">=2.0.0"
  - name: community.general
    version: ">=9.0.0,<10.0.0"
roles:
  - name: geerlingguy.nginx

Worked example
The lab’s site.yml uses the lemonade_web role in four lines:
- name: Configure the web servers
  hosts: web
  gather_facts: false
  roles:
    - lemonade_web
The output shows each task prefixed with the role name, TASK [lemonade_web : Render the nginx config], so you always know which role a line came from. To reuse the role at the beach stand, point a new inventory at the same playbook. The role does not change.

title: 9. Roles and Collections
text:
Rules and conventions

One role, one job: lemonade_web, lemonade_db, common. Avoid a “do everything” role.
Every input in defaults/, documented in README.md and typed in argument_specs.yml.
Prefix variables with the role name, so two roles never fight over port.
Use import_* by default and include_* only when you need run-time decisions or loops.
Pin collection versions in requirements.yml, so a new release cannot surprise you.
Write FQCNs everywhere, even for ansible.builtin.

Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




A user-facing value in vars/main.yml
group_vars overrides are ignored.
Move it to defaults/main.yml.


when: on import_role, expecting one check
The condition is evaluated on every inner task, sometimes with surprising results.
Use include_role to decide once.

Inner tasks don’t get the tag, and --tags skips them.
Use import_role, or apply: { tags: [...] }.


Listing a role twice to run it twice
It runs once.
Give different parameters, or allow_duplicates: true.

couldn't resolve module/action 'community.general.ufw'
ansible-galaxy collection install -r requirements.yml.

title: 9. Roles and Collections
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
Defaults versus vars. Using the precedence rule from lesson 6, a role default has rank \(r_d = 2\) and a role var has rank \(r_v = 15\). An inventory host variable has rank \(r_h = 9\). So
\[
r_d < r_h < r_v
\]
where \(r_d\), \(r_h\) and \(r_v\) are the ranks of a role default, an inventory host variable and a role variable.
Example. If lemonade_nginx_workers is in defaults/ (1) and host_vars/web1.yml (4), then \(\max(2, 9) = 9\) wins: 4. Move the default to vars/ and the winner becomes \(\max(15, 9) = 15\): 1, and the host override is silently lost. That is why user-facing values belong in defaults/.
How many times a role runs. In one play, list a role \(k\) times with parameter sets \(p_1, \dots, p_k\). Without allow_duplicates:
\[
\operatorname{runs} = \big\lvert \lbrace p_1, p_2, \dots, p_k \rbrace \big\rvert
\]
where:

\(p_i\) is the set of parameters passed on the \(i\)-th listing (empty if none);
\(\lbrace \dots \rbrace\) makes a set, so identical parameter sets count once;
\(\lvert \cdot \rvert\) is the number of elements in the set.

Example. A test play listed a small role three times: greet, greet, and { role: greet, greet_port: 9090 }. The parameter sets are \(p_1 = \lbrace\rbrace\), \(p_2 = \lbrace\rbrace\) and \(p_3 = \lbrace \text{port} = 9090 \rbrace\). The set \(\lbrace p_1, p_2, p_3 \rbrace = \lbrace \lbrace\rbrace, \lbrace \text{port} = 9090 \rbrace \rbrace\) has 2 elements, and the real run printed exactly two messages: port 8080 and port 9090.
Version ranges. The requirement >=9.0.0,<10.0.0 is a half-open interval:
\[
v \in [\,9.0.0,\ 10.0.0\,)
\]
where \(v\) is the collection version, \([\) means the left end is included and \()\) means the right end is excluded, with versions compared part by part (major, then minor, then patch).
Example. 9.0.0 is allowed (left end included). 9.5.2 is allowed, since \(9 = 9\) and the major part is below 10. 10.0.0 is not allowed (right end excluded), so a breaking major release cannot slip in.

title: Ansible
text:
You have three servers. You want every one of them set up the same way: the same packages, the same config files, the same users. Doing it by hand means logging in to each server and typing the same commands. You make mistakes, and nobody can see later what you did.
Ansible writes those steps down as a text file and runs them on many servers at once. Run the file again and Ansible only changes what is still wrong. You can keep the file in Git, review it and run it again next year.
This part of the book teaches Ansible through one running example.

title: Ansible
section: The running example: the Lemonade Stand
text:
The running example: the Lemonade Stand
The Lemonade Stand is a tiny web app that shows a menu of drinks and prices. It runs on three servers:
                     you (control node: your laptop)
                                 │  ansible-playbook site.yml
             ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
             ▼                   ▼                   ▼
   web1  192.0.2.11      web2  192.0.2.12      db1  192.0.2.21
   group: web, prod      group: web, prod      group: db, prod
   nginx :80 → app :8080 nginx :80 → app :8080 database settings

web1 and web2 are in the group web. Each runs nginx on port 80, which forwards requests to the Lemonade app on port 8080.
db1 is in the group db.
All three are in the group prod (production).
The addresses come from 192.0.2.0/24, a range reserved for documentation, so they never clash with a real network.

title: Ansible
section: Run the lab on your laptop
text:
Run the lab on your laptop
The lab pretends to be the whole fleet on one machine. Every host uses ansible_connection: local, and each writes into its own folder under /tmp/lemonade-lab/. You need no SSH, no sudo and no virtual machines.
pipx install ansible-core          # or: brew install ansible
cd devops/ansible/examples
ansible all -m ansible.builtin.ping
ansible-playbook site.yml
ansible-playbook site.yml          # second run reports changed=0
Lab files: ansible.cfg · inventory.yml · site.yml · roles/lemonade_web/ · rolling-update.yml · vault-demo.yml.

title: Ansible
text:
Lessons
Read them in order. Each lesson starts with a problem from the Lemonade Stand, explains the idea for a ten-year-old, lists every keyword with its rules, shows real output from the lab, and ends with the maths behind it.

How Ansible works: control node, managed nodes, SSH, modules, desired state, idempotency.
Inventory: hosts, groups, connection variables, group_vars, host patterns.
Ad hoc commands: one-off tasks with ansible, and every common flag.
Playbooks: YAML rules, play and task keywords, ansible-playbook flags, PLAY RECAP.
Essential modules: the 30 modules you will use most.
Variables and facts: where values come from and which one wins.
Jinja2 templates: expressions, filters, tests, lookups, config files.
Conditionals, loops and handlers: when, loop, until, notify, block.
Roles and collections: packaging work for reuse.

title: 10. Vault and Secrets
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipThe secret decoder ring



In the 1930s, children who listened to the Little Orphan Annie radio show could send away for a secret decoder ring. At the end of each show the announcer read out a string of numbers. To everyone else it was nonsense. With the ring you could turn the numbers back into the message. (The 1983 film A Christmas Story has a famous scene about it.)
Ansible Vault is a decoder ring for your passwords. The encrypted file can sit in Git where everybody sees it, because without the vault password it is just a wall of numbers. Only Ansible, holding the password, turns it back into the real secret, and only while the playbook runs.

title: 10. Vault and Secrets
text:
The concept, precisely

ansible-vault encrypts a whole YAML file, or a single string, with a password you choose.
The encryption is AES-256 (format 1.1: AES in counter mode, plus an HMAC-SHA256 checksum, with the key derived from your password by PBKDF2 using 10,000 rounds).
An encrypted file starts with a header line: $ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.1;AES256.
When a playbook loads an encrypted file, Ansible decrypts it in memory. The plain text is never written to disk.
A vault ID is a label for one password, such as dev or prod, so different environments can use different passwords. The header then includes the label: $ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.2;AES256;prod.

title: 10. Vault and Secrets
text:
Every ansible-vault subcommand









Subcommand
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




create FILE
Opens your editor on a new file and saves it encrypted.
Uses $EDITOR; needs a terminal.
ansible-vault create group_vars/db/vault.yml


edit FILE
Decrypts into your editor, then re-encrypts on save.
The plain text only exists in a temporary file while you edit.
ansible-vault edit group_vars/db/vault.yml


view FILE
Prints the decrypted content.
Nothing is written to disk.
ansible-vault view secrets/vault.yml


encrypt FILE…
Encrypts existing plain files in place.
Check git diff first, so the plain version is never committed.
ansible-vault encrypt secrets/vault.yml


decrypt FILE…
Turns encrypted files back into plain files on disk.
Rarely needed. Prefer view or edit.
ansible-vault decrypt secrets/vault.yml


rekey FILE…
Changes the password of encrypted files.
Do this when someone with the password leaves the team.
ansible-vault rekey secrets/vault.yml


encrypt_string
Encrypts one value and prints YAML you can paste.
Use --name to print the variable name too.
ansible-vault encrypt_string 'lemonade-demo-secret' --name vault_db_password

text:
Every password option









Option
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




-J, --ask-vault-pass
Prompts for the password.
For people at a keyboard.
ansible-playbook site.yml -J


--vault-password-file FILE
Reads the password from a file.
The file must not be in Git. If it is executable, Ansible runs it and reads its output.
--vault-password-file ~/.lemonade-vault-pass


--vault-id LABEL@SOURCE
A labelled password. SOURCE is a file, a script, or prompt.
Repeat it for several environments.
--vault-id dev@prompt --vault-id prod@~/.prod-pass


--encrypt-vault-id LABEL
Which label to encrypt with, when several are given.

--encrypt-vault-id prod


--new-vault-password-file
The new password for rekey.

rekey f.yml --new-vault-password-file new.txt


--output FILE
Write the result elsewhere instead of in place.
- means standard output.
decrypt f.yml --output -


ANSIBLE_VAULT_PASSWORD_FILE
Environment variable for the password file.
Handy in CI.
export ANSIBLE_VAULT_PASSWORD_FILE=~/.pass


vault_password_file (ansible.cfg)
Default password file for the project.
Never point it at a file inside the repository.
vault_password_file = ~/.lemonade-vault-pass

title: 10. Vault and Secrets
text:
The vault_ naming convention
Split each group’s variables into two files:
# group_vars/db/vars.yml   (plain text: shows WHICH secrets exist)
db_password: "{{ vault_db_password }}"
# group_vars/db/vault.yml  (encrypted: holds the VALUES)
vault_db_password: lemonade-demo-secret
Why bother with two names?

grep -r db_password still finds where the variable is defined, even though the value is encrypted.
A reviewer sees in the plain file that a new secret was added.
Every encrypted value starts with vault_, so you can tell at a glance which variables are secret.

The lab keeps both files in secrets/ and loads them with vars_files, so that site.yml runs without any password.

title: 10. Vault and Secrets
text:
Hiding secrets in output: no_log
Encryption protects the file. It does not stop Ansible from printing the value. With -v, a task’s arguments and results appear in the output and in CI logs. Add no_log: true to every task that handles a secret.








Keyword
What it does
Example




no_log: true
Replaces the task’s arguments and result with a censored message.
on the task that writes the password file


no_log: true on a play or block
Applies it to every task inside.
- block: [...] with no_log: true

text:
Worked example
From devops/ansible/examples/, with the throwaway demo password:
ansible-vault view secrets/vault.yml --vault-password-file secrets/demo-vault-password.txt
vault_db_password: lemonade-demo-secret
The file in Git, by contrast:
$ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.1;AES256
30373062373033323263306336656637373639653561323337313730316136613164313237383331
6162616635363265373731343938636665396433303866310a346665373433656133613631366661
...
The lab’s vault-demo.yml:
- name: Use an encrypted password without printing it
  hosts: db
  gather_facts: false
  vars_files: [secrets/vars.yml, secrets/vault.yml]
  tasks:
    - name: Write the password file
      ansible.builtin.copy:
        content: "{{ db_password }}\n"
        dest: "{{ lab_root }}/{{ inventory_hostname }}/db.password"
        mode: "0600"
      no_log: true
    - name: Show only the length
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "The password has {{ db_password | length }} characters"
ansible-playbook vault-demo.yml --vault-password-file secrets/demo-vault-password.txt
TASK [Write the password file] *************************************************
changed: [db1]
TASK [Show only the length] ****************************************************
ok: [db1] =>
    msg: The password has 20 characters
Without the password, Ansible refuses to start:
Attempting to decrypt but no vault secrets found.
Origin: .../examples/secrets/vault.yml
Other subcommands, all tested with throwaway passwords:
ansible-vault rekey vault.yml --vault-password-file pass.txt --new-vault-password-file newpass.txt
# Rekey successful
ansible-vault encrypt prod.yml --vault-id prod@pass.txt && head -1 prod.yml
# $ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.2;AES256;prod
ansible-vault encrypt_string 'lemonade-demo-secret' --name vault_db_password --vault-password-file pass.txt

#           $ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.1;AES256
#           61343062353832626430...

title: 10. Vault and Secrets
text:
Rules and conventions

Never commit a real vault password file. Keep it in a password manager, or in your CI system’s secret store. (The lab’s demo password file is committed only because it protects a fake value.)
One vault ID per environment: dev, staging and prod should have different passwords.
Use the vars.yml + vault.yml pair with the vault_ prefix.
Add no_log: true to every task that uses a secret.
Use view and edit, not decrypt, so plain text never sits in your working copy.

title: 2. Inventory
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipThe class register



A teacher has a register: a list of every child in the school. Children are also in groups. Maya is in Class 4B and in the chess club.
When the head teacher says “Class 4B, go to the hall”, only 4B moves. When she says “everyone in the chess club who is also in 4B”, only the children in both lists move. When she says “the whole school except the chess club”, everyone moves except the chess players.
An Ansible inventory is that register. Hosts are the children. Groups are the classes and clubs. A host pattern is the head teacher’s instruction for who should move.

title: 2. Inventory
text:
The concept, precisely

A host is one machine Ansible manages. Its inventory name, such as web1, is just a label. The real address goes in ansible_host.
A group is a named set of hosts. A host can be in many groups.
A group can contain other groups. They are its children. prod contains web and db, so every web or db host is also in prod.
Two groups always exist. all contains every host. ungrouped contains hosts that are in no group except all.
Inventory variables attach values to a host or a group, such as the SSH user or the app port.


The same fleet in two formats
INI format, short and flat:
[web]
web1 ansible_host=192.0.2.11
web2 ansible_host=192.0.2.12

[db]
db1 ansible_host=192.0.2.21

[prod:children]
web
db
YAML format, the lab’s inventory.yml:
all:
  children:
    web:
      hosts:
        web1: { ansible_host: 192.0.2.11 }
        web2: { ansible_host: 192.0.2.12 }
    db:
      hosts:
        db1: { ansible_host: 192.0.2.21 }
    prod:
      children:
        web:
        db:
Both describe exactly the same groups. YAML is easier to read when hosts have many variables. INI is quicker to type.

Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




[name] (INI)
Starts a group.
Lowercase letters, digits and _. Avoid -, because it is not a valid variable name in Jinja.
[web]

[prod:children]

A map of group names.

Variables for every host in the group.

section: Variables in files: group_vars/ and host_vars/
text:
Variables in files: group_vars/ and host_vars/
Putting many variables inside the inventory gets messy. Ansible also reads two folders next to the inventory (or next to the playbook):
examples/
├── inventory.yml
├── group_vars/
│   ├── all.yml      # every host:   lab_root: /tmp/lemonade-lab
│   ├── web.yml      # group "web":  lemonade_menu: [...]
│   └── db.yml       # group "db":   db_port: 5432
└── host_vars/
    └── web1.yml     # only web1:    lemonade_nginx_workers: 4







Rule
Detail




File name = group or host name
group_vars/web.yml applies to group web. host_vars/web1.yml applies to host web1.


A folder works too
group_vars/db/vars.yml and group_vars/db/vault.yml are both loaded for group db.


Host beats group
A value in host_vars/web1.yml overrides the same name in group_vars/web.yml.


Child group beats parent
A value in group_vars/web.yml overrides group_vars/prod.yml, because web is a child of prod.


Same-level tie
Groups at the same depth are merged in alphabetical order, so the last name wins. Set ansible_group_priority to change this.



Lesson 6 gives the full precedence order.

title: 2. Inventory
text:
Rules and conventions

Name hosts by role and number (web1, db1) and put real addresses in ansible_host.
One inventory per environment: inventories/staging/ and inventories/prod/. Then a typo cannot send a staging change to production.
Use groups for roles and environments: web, db, prod, staging. Target groups, not single hosts.
Keep variables in group_vars/ and host_vars/, not in long inventory lines.
Always quote patterns that contain &, ! or *.
Check before you run: --list-hosts shows exactly which hosts a pattern selects.

text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Group name with a dash, web-servers
Warning “Invalid characters were found in group names”.
Use web_servers.


Unquoted prod:!db in zsh or bash
event not found
Use single quotes: 'prod:!db'.


group_vars in the wrong folder
Variables are silently missing.
Put it next to the inventory file or the playbook. Check with ansible-inventory --host web1.


Expecting all[0:1] to give one host
Two hosts run.
Slices include both ends. Use all[0] for one host.


Forgetting the trailing comma in -i web1
Ansible looks for a file called web1.
Write -i web1,.

title: 2. Inventory
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
A group is a set of hosts, and patterns are set operations.
\[
\begin{aligned}
A \texttt{:} B &= A \cup B \\
A \texttt{:\&} B &= A \cap B \\
A \texttt{:!} B &= A \setminus B
\end{aligned}
\]
where:

\(A\) and \(B\) are sets of hosts, such as the group web or prod;
\(A \cup B\) (union) is every host in \(A\) or \(B\);
\(A \cap B\) (intersection) is every host in both \(A\) and \(B\);
\(A \setminus B\) (difference) is every host in \(A\) that is not in \(B\).

Example. In the lab, \(W = \lbrace \texttt{web1}, \texttt{web2} \rbrace\) is web, \(D = \lbrace \texttt{db1} \rbrace\) is db, and \(P = W \cup D = \lbrace \texttt{web1}, \texttt{web2}, \texttt{db1} \rbrace\) is prod.

prod:&web is \(P \cap W = \lbrace \texttt{web1}, \texttt{web2} \rbrace\).
prod:!db is \(P \setminus D = \lbrace \texttt{web1}, \texttt{web2} \rbrace\).

When you mix the operators, Ansible does not read them from left to right. It first joins every union term, then intersects, then removes the exclusions:
\[
\text{pattern} = \Big( \bigcup_{i} U_i \Big) \cap \Big( \bigcap_{j} I_j \Big) \setminus \Big( \bigcup_{k} E_k \Big)
\]
where:

\(U_i\) are the plain terms (no prefix), such as web and db;
\(I_j\) are the terms written with &, such as ∏
\(E_k\) are the terms written with !, such as !web2;
the \(\bigcup\) and \(\bigcap\) signs mean “union of all of them” and “intersection of all of them”.

Example. For web:db:&prod:!web2:

Unions: \(U_1 \cup U_2 = W \cup D = \lbrace \texttt{web1}, \texttt{web2}, \texttt{db1} \rbrace\).
Intersection: \(\cap\, P\) keeps all three, because all are in prod.
Exclusion: \(\setminus \lbrace \texttt{web2} \rbrace\) leaves \(\lbrace \texttt{web1}, \texttt{db1} \rbrace\).

That matches the real --list-hosts output above. Writing '!web2:web:db' gives the same two hosts, because the order of the terms does not matter.
A range in the inventory expands to a count of hosts:
\[
n = b - a + 1
\]
where \(a\) is the first number and \(b\) the last number inside name[a:b], and \(n\) is the number of hosts created.
Example. web[1:3] has \(a = 1\) and \(b = 3\), so \(n = 3 - 1 + 1 = 3\) hosts: web1, web2, web3. A slice pattern all[0:1] follows the same rule: \(1 - 0 + 1 = 2\) hosts, which is why it returned web1 and web2.

text:
Version 1.1.0 of the Lemonade app is ready. If you upgrade web1 and web2 at the same time, both reload together and customers see errors for a moment. Worse: if 1.1.0 is broken, both servers are broken, and the stand is closed.

upgrade it,

then move to the next server, and stop at the first failure.

title: 11. Rolling Deployments
text:
Version 1.1.0 of the Lemonade app is ready. If you upgrade web1 and web2 at the same time, both reload together and customers see errors for a moment. Worse: if 1.1.0 is broken, both servers are broken, and the stand is closed.
You want to:

take one server out of the load balancer,
upgrade it,
check that it really works,
put it back,
then move to the next server, and stop at the first failure.

title: 11. Rolling Deployments
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipSwapping football players



In a football match the coach never takes all the players off at once. That would leave the pitch empty and the other team would score. Instead the coach makes substitutions: one player comes off, a fresh player goes on, and the team keeps playing the whole time.
If the new player twists an ankle in the first minute, the coach stops making substitutions and thinks again.
A rolling deployment is a substitution plan for servers. serial: 1 means “swap one server at a time”. max_fail_percentage: 0 means “if any new player gets hurt, stop the substitutions”.

title: 11. Rolling Deployments
text:
The concept, precisely

Normally a play runs each task on all its hosts before moving to the next task.
With serial, Ansible splits the hosts into batches and runs the whole play on one batch before starting the next. In the output, the PLAY [...] header repeats once per batch.
After each task, Ansible checks the share of failed hosts in the current batch. If it is above max_fail_percentage, the whole run stops, and later batches are never touched.
Tasks that act on another machine, such as a load balancer, use delegate_to.
Notified handlers run at the end of each section in each batch, so a server is reloaded before its health check.

title: 11. Rolling Deployments
text:
Every rolling-update keyword









Keyword
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




serial: N
Batches of N hosts.
1 is the safest; the last batch may be smaller.
serial: 1


serial: "P%"
Batches of P percent of the play’s hosts.
Rounded down, but at least 1 host.
serial: "30%"


serial: [a, b, c]
Growing batches: first a, then b, then c for the rest.
The last value repeats until all hosts are done. Classic canary: [1, "30%", "100%"].
serial: [1, 5, 10]


max_fail_percentage
Stop when the failed share of a batch is greater than this.
0 stops at the first failure.
max_fail_percentage: 0


any_errors_fatal
Stop the play on all hosts as soon as any host fails.
Works with or without serial. The failing task finishes on the current batch, then nothing else runs.
any_errors_fatal: true


delegate_to
Run this task on another host, with the current host’s variables.
For load balancers, monitoring and DNS.
delegate_to: lb1


run_once
Run the task on one host only, once per batch.
Combine with delegate_to for one-off work.
run_once: true


throttle
At most N hosts run this task at the same time.
Cannot go above forks or serial.
throttle: 1


strategy: linear
Every host finishes a task before the next task starts.
The default. Required for max_fail_percentage.
strategy: linear


strategy: free
Each host runs at its own speed.
Faster, but max_fail_percentage is not supported.
strategy: free


order
Which hosts go first.
inventory, sorted, reverse_sorted, reverse_inventory, shuffle.
order: sorted


ansible_play_batch
Magic variable: the hosts in this batch.

{ ansible_play_batch }




The health-check modules



Module
What it waits for
Example




ansible.builtin.wait_for
A port to open or close, or text to appear in a file.
wait_for: { port: 8080, timeout: 30 }


ansible.builtin.uri + until
An HTTP status, retried.
until: health.status == 200 (lesson 8)

title: 11. Rolling Deployments
text:
Worked example
The heart of the lab’s rolling-update.yml is the play header:
- name: Upgrade the web servers one at a time
  hosts: web
  gather_facts: false
  serial: 1                  # one server per batch
  max_fail_percentage: 0     # any failure stops the rollout
And the drain → upgrade → check → enable pattern, written as pre_tasks, roles and post_tasks. (The full file also has a first pre-task, “Create the load balancer folder”, with run_once: true, and a last post-task that removes the .off file.)
  pre_tasks:
    - name: Take this server out of the load balancer
      ansible.builtin.file: { path: "{{ lab_root }}/lb/{{ inventory_hostname }}.off", state: touch }
      delegate_to: localhost
  roles:
    - lemonade_web
  post_tasks:
    - name: Wait until the menu shows the new version
      ansible.builtin.wait_for:
        path: "{{ lab_root }}/{{ inventory_hostname }}/site/index.html"
        search_regex: "version {{ lemonade_version }}"
Run it:
ansible-playbook rolling-update.yml -e lemonade_version=1.1.0
Real output, trimmed. Notice that the PLAY header appears twice, once per batch:
PLAY [Upgrade the web servers one at a time] ***********************************
TASK [Create the load balancer folder] *****************************************
changed: [web1 -> localhost]
TASK [Take this server out of the load balancer] *******************************
changed: [web1 -> localhost]
TASK [lemonade_web : Render the menu page] *************************************
changed: [web1]
RUNNING HANDLER [lemonade_web : Reload nginx] **********************************
ok: [web1] =>
    msg: nginx reloaded on web1
TASK [Wait until the menu shows the new version] *******************************
ok: [web1]
TASK [Put this server back into the load balancer] *****************************
changed: [web1 -> localhost]

PLAY [Upgrade the web servers one at a time] ***********************************
TASK [Create the load balancer folder] *****************************************
ok: [web2 -> localhost]
...
PLAY RECAP *********************************************************************
web1   : ok=8    changed=4    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0
web2   : ok=8    changed=3    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0
Three things to see:

web1 -> localhost means the task ran on the control node (the “load balancer”) on behalf of web1.
The handler ran inside the batch, before the health check.
“Create the load balancer folder” has run_once: true, yet it ran in both batches: changed for web1, then ok for web2. run_once means once per batch.

Dry run first. --check --diff shows the version change and skips wait_for, which cannot be predicted:
-<p>Served by web1, version 1.1.0</p>
+<p>Served by web1, version 1.2.0</p>
changed: [web1]
TASK [Wait until the menu shows the new version] *******************************
skipping: [web1]
On real servers the drain step talks to the real load balancer, and the check calls the app:
- name: Drain this server in HAProxy
  community.general.haproxy: { state: disabled, host: "{{ inventory_hostname }}", backend: lemonade }
  delegate_to: lb1
- name: Wait for the app's health endpoint
  ansible.builtin.uri: { url: "http://{{ ansible_host }}:8080/health" }
  register: health
  until: health.status == 200
  retries: 10
  delay: 3

title: 11. Rolling Deployments
text:
Rules and conventions

Keep the version in Git (group_vars/web.yml), not only in -e. Otherwise the next site.yml run puts the default version back. You can see this in the lab: after a rolling update with -e lemonade_version=1.1.0, a plain site.yml --check wants to change the menu back to 1.0.0.
Drain, upgrade, verify, enable, in that order, every time.
Start small: serial: [1, "30%", "100%"] upgrades one canary server first.
Fail fast: max_fail_percentage: 0 for web servers; consider any_errors_fatal: true for database schema changes.
Health checks must test the app, not just the port. A port can be open while the app returns errors.
Leave headroom: never take out more servers than the rest can carry (see the maths below).

title: 11. Rolling Deployments
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




No serial
All web servers reload at once; brief outage.
serial: 1 or a percentage.


max_fail_percentage: 50 with serial: 2
One failed server in a batch of two does not stop the run (50% is not above 50).
Use 0, or 49 if you want “stop at 1 of 2”.


strategy: free with max_fail_percentage
Warning: not supported with the free strategy.
Use the default linear strategy.


run_once expecting “once per play” with serial
The task runs once in every batch.
Move it into its own play without serial.


Enabling the server before the health check
A broken server receives traffic.
The health check must come before “put back”.


Version only passed with -e
The next site.yml reverts the version.
Store it in group_vars.

title: 5. Essential Modules
text:
Ansible ships with thousands of modules. A beginner does not know where to start, so they write everything with shell:. Then every run reports changed, --check cannot predict anything, and handlers fire every time.
For the Lemonade Stand you need perhaps thirty modules: write files, install nginx, start services, create a user, call the health endpoint. This lesson is the map.

text:
Ansible ships with thousands of modules. A beginner does not know where to start, so they write everything with shell:. Then every run reports changed, --check cannot predict anything, and handlers fire every time.
For the Lemonade Stand you need perhaps thirty modules: write files, install nginx, start services, create a user, call the health endpoint. This lesson is the map.

title: 5. Essential Modules
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipA box of LEGO pieces



A module is one LEGO piece with a single job. A wheel rolls. A hinge bends. A window lets light in. You don’t carve a wheel out of a plain brick. You pick the wheel piece, because it already works.
shell is the plain brick: you can build anything with it, but you have to shape it yourself, and it never tells you whether anything changed. Grab the special piece first: copy for files, package for software, service for programs that keep running. Use the plain brick only when no special piece exists.

title: 5. Essential Modules
text:
The concept, precisely

A module is a small program with parameters (its inputs) and return values (a JSON result).
Every module returns at least changed (true or false) and failed. Many add more, such as rc and stdout for command, or stat.exists for stat.
Save the result with register: and use it in later tasks (lesson 6).
Write the fully qualified collection name (FQCN): namespace.collection.module. All modules below live in ansible.builtin, which ships with ansible-core.
Most modules are declarative and idempotent. The exceptions, marked ⚠, always run.

Find modules and read their documentation without leaving the terminal:








Command
What it does
Example




ansible-doc -l
List every installed module.
ansible-doc -l ansible.builtin (71 modules in 2.21)


ansible-doc NAME
Full documentation: parameters, return values, examples.
ansible-doc ansible.builtin.copy


ansible-doc -s NAME
A short task snippet with every parameter.
ansible-doc -s ansible.builtin.lineinfile


ansible-doc -t TYPE -l
List other plugin types.
ansible-doc -t lookup -l

title: 5. Essential Modules
text:
Worked examples
A web server from nothing: the four steps that every web role has. Packages and services need root, so the play sets become: true.
- name: Install nginx
  ansible.builtin.package: { name: nginx, state: present }

- name: Write the Lemonade site
  ansible.builtin.template:
    src: nginx.conf.j2
    dest: /etc/nginx/conf.d/lemonade.conf
    validate: nginx -t -c %s
  notify: Reload nginx

- name: Keep nginx running after reboots
  ansible.builtin.service: { name: nginx, state: started, enabled: true }
A health check that reads the page. Run against a local copy of the menu page:
- name: Ask the menu page for a 200
  ansible.builtin.uri:
    url: http://127.0.0.1:18080/index.html
    return_content: true
  register: menu

- ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg: "{{ menu.status }} {{ 'Pink Lemonade' in menu.content }}"
ok: [localhost] =>
    msg: 200 True
Asking for a page that does not exist fails, because 404 is not in status_code:
fatal: [localhost]: FAILED! =>
    msg: 'Status code was 404 and not [200]: HTTP Error 404: File not found'
    status: 404
Two modules fighting over one file. Each task below is idempotent on its own:
- ansible.builtin.copy:
    dest: prices.conf
    content: "classic = 2.50\n"      # add "force: false" to fix the fight
- ansible.builtin.lineinfile:
    path: prices.conf
    line: "pink = 3.00"
Three runs in a row report changed=2, changed=2, changed=2. copy resets the file to one line, and then lineinfile adds the second line back. With force: false, copy only creates the file when it is missing, and the runs report changed=0.

title: 5. Essential Modules
text:
Rules and conventions

Pick the most specific module. package over shell: apt-get, copy over shell: echo >.
Always write the FQCN, so readers and ansible-lint know where the module comes from.
One owner per file. Either template manages the whole file, or lineinfile/blockinfile manage parts of it. Never both.
Quote file modes: mode: "0644" (lesson 4).
Validate config files with validate: before they go live.
Make command and shell honest with creates, removes or changed_when.
Read ansible-doc for the return values before you write register:.

title: 5. Essential Modules
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




shell: systemctl restart nginx in normal tasks
Restarts on every run; changed every time.
service with state: started in tasks, state: restarted in a handler.


copy and lineinfile on one file
The playbook is never changed=0.
Give the file one owner, or use force: false on copy.


user: { groups: www-data } without append
The user loses its other groups, such as sudo.
Add append: true.


apt without update_cache on a new server
No package matching 'nginx' is available.
update_cache: true and cache_valid_time: 3600.


package without state
Behaviour depends on the OS package manager behind it; the docs mark state as required.
Always write state: present.


Host has no Python
Every module fails.
Bootstrap with raw: apt-get install -y python3.

title: 5. Essential Modules
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
A playbook runs its tasks one after another. As functions on the server state, that is a composition:
\[
R = t_n \circ \cdots \circ t_2 \circ t_1
\]
where:

\(t_1, t_2, \dots, t_n\) are the tasks in order; each is a function from states to states (lesson 1);
\(\circ\) means “do the right-hand function first, then the left-hand one”, so \((t_2 \circ t_1)(s) = t_2(t_1(s))\);
\(R\) is the whole run.

Example. The fight above has \(n = 2\) tasks: \(t_1\) is copy and \(t_2\) is lineinfile, so \(R = t_2 \circ t_1\) and \(R(s) = t_2(t_1(s))\). Starting from an empty folder \(s\): \(t_1(s)\) is a file with the one line classic = 2.50, and \(t_2\) of that adds pink = 3.00. So \(R(s)\) is the two-line file.
Even when every \(t_i\) is idempotent, \(R\) can still report changes on every run. Ansible reports task \(i\) as changed when it altered the state it was given:
\[
C = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \big[\, t_i(s_{i-1}) \neq s_{i-1} \,\big], \qquad s_i = t_i(s_{i-1})
\]
where:

\(s_0\) is the state before the run, and \(s_i\) is the state after task \(i\);
\([\,P\,]\) is 1 when the statement \(P\) is true and 0 when it is false;
\(C\) is the changed= count for this host.

Example, the fight above. Let \(s^\ast\) be the finished file with two lines, classic = 2.50 and pink = 3.00. Start the second run from \(s_0 = s^\ast\):

\(t_1\) = copy with force: true: \(t_1(s^\ast)\) is the one-line file, which is different from \(s^\ast\). That counts 1.
\(t_2\) = lineinfile: it adds pink = 3.00 back, which is different from the one-line file. That counts 1.
\(C = 1 + 1 = 2\), and the final state is \(s^\ast\) again.

So \(R(R(s)) = R(s)\): the file ends the same. But \(C = 2\) on every run, so a handler would fire every time. With force: false, \(t_1(s^\ast) = s^\ast\) and \(t_2(s^\ast) = s^\ast\), so \(C = 0 + 0 = 0\). A playbook is only truly idempotent when both the state and the change count settle.

title: 6. Variables and Facts
text:
The Lemonade web servers are almost identical, but not quite:

web1 is a bigger machine and should run 4 nginx workers. web2 should use the normal 1.
Every web server serves the same menu.
During a test you want to try 8 workers once, without editing any file.

If the same playbook must produce slightly different results, the differences go into variables. Then the question is: when a value is set in several places, which one wins?

title: 6. Variables and Facts
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipSchool rules and the loudspeaker



At school there are rules at different levels:

The school rule: “Lunch is at 12:00.”
Your class rule: “Class 4B has lunch at 12:30.”
A note just for you: “Maya, you have lunch at 11:45 because of your dentist visit.”
The head teacher’s loudspeaker announcement: “Today everyone has lunch at 13:00!”

When rules disagree, the more specific one wins: your note beats the class rule, and the class rule beats the school rule. The loudspeaker beats everything.
Ansible variables work the same way. Role defaults are the school rule, group_vars is the class rule, host_vars is the note just for you, and -e on the command line is the loudspeaker.

title: 6. Variables and Facts
text:
The concept, precisely

A variable is a name with a value. Use it in Jinja as { lemonade_app_port }.
Values can be strings, numbers, booleans, lists or dictionaries. Read inside a dictionary with menu.price or menu['price'].
Facts are variables Ansible discovers on each host: its OS, IP addresses, memory and so on.
Magic variables are variables Ansible sets itself, such as inventory_hostname.
Registered variables hold the result of a task (register:).


Naming rules



Rule
Valid
Invalid




Letters, digits and underscores only
lemonade_app_port
lemonade-app-port, app port, app.port


Start with a letter or _
web_port
8080_port


Not a Python keyword or playbook keyword
menu_items
class, async, environment, hosts


Prefix role variables with the role name
lemonade_menu
menu (too easy to clash)


Prefix secrets with vault_
vault_db_password
(lesson 10)

title: 6. Variables and Facts
section: Every place a variable can come from
text:
Every place a variable can come from









Source
Where it lives
Rule / convention
Example




Role defaults
roles/x/defaults/main.yml
Lowest precedence. Put every tunable value here.
lemonade_nginx_workers: 1


Inventory
vars: in inventory.yml
Prefer group_vars/ files.
all: vars: { ansible_connection: local }


group_vars/
next to inventory or playbook
One file or folder per group.
group_vars/web.yml


host_vars/
next to inventory or playbook
One file or folder per host.
host_vars/web1.yml


Facts
gathered by setup
Read with ansible_facts['…'].
ansible_facts['distribution']


Play vars
in the play
For values that belong to this playbook only.
vars: { lemonade_version: "1.1.0" }


vars_files
listed in the play
Usually secrets.
vars_files: [secrets/vault.yml]


vars_prompt
in the play
Asks a person; blocks automation.
vars_prompt: [{ name: release }]


Role vars
roles/x/vars/main.yml
High precedence. For constants users must not change.
lemonade_folders: [nginx, site]


Block and task vars
on a block or task
Only visible there.
vars: { greeting: hi }


include_vars
a task
Loads a file at run time.
include_vars: { file: "{{ ansible_facts['os_family'] }}.yml" }


set_fact / register
a task
Created while the play runs.
register: menu_check


Role parameters
roles: [{ role: x, var: 1 }]
For one use of a role.
- { role: lemonade_web, lemonade_app_port: 9090 }


Extra vars
-e on the command line
Always wins.
-e lemonade_nginx_workers=8




The precedence ladder
The official documentation lists 22 levels. From lowest (1) to highest (22):

command-line values such as -u deploy (these are not variables)
role defaults
inventory file or script group vars
inventory group_vars/all
playbook group_vars/all
inventory group_vars/*
playbook group_vars/*
inventory file or script host vars
inventory host_vars/*
playbook host_vars/*
host facts and cached set_fact
play vars
play vars_prompt
play vars_files
role vars (vars/main.yml)
block vars
task vars
include_vars
set_fact and registered vars
role (and include_role) parameters
include parameters
extra vars (-e)

You rarely need all 22. Remember the short version: defaults < group < host < play < role vars < task < set_fact < -e.
Two more rules matter:

Dictionaries and lists are replaced, not merged. The lab’s role default menu has one drink and group_vars/web.yml has three. The web servers get exactly three, not four. Merge on purpose with the combine filter (lesson 7).
Variables are per host. web1 and web2 each have their own lemonade_nginx_workers.

text:
Facts
With gather_facts: true (the default), each play starts with a hidden setup task that fills ansible_facts.









Keyword or setting
What it does
Rule / convention
Example




gather_facts
Run setup at the start of the play.
Turn off when you don’t read facts.
gather_facts: false


gather_subset
Collect only some facts.
min is fast; !hardware skips one area.
gather_subset: [min, network]

Read a fact.
The preferred form. The key has no ansible_ prefix.
ansible_facts['distribution']


ansible_x
Old top-level form.
Deprecated: 2.21 warns, and the default changes in 2.24.

Show only matching facts.
Ad hoc exploration.
-a "filter=ansible_python_version"


/etc/ansible/facts.d/*.fact
Custom facts on the host.
JSON or INI files, read into ansible_local.
ansible_local['lemonade']['version']


fact_caching (ansible.cfg)
Remember facts between runs.
jsonfile or redis; fact_caching_timeout is in seconds.
fact_caching = jsonfile

title: 6. Variables and Facts
text:
Worked example: who wins?
lemonade_nginx_workers is set in two files:
# roles/lemonade_web/defaults/main.yml   (level 2)
lemonade_nginx_workers: 1
# host_vars/web1.yml                     (level 9)
lemonade_nginx_workers: 4
web1 gets 4 and web2 falls back to 1. Now add the loudspeaker for one dry run:
ansible-playbook site.yml --limit web --check --diff -e lemonade_nginx_workers=8
TASK [lemonade_web : Render the nginx config] **********************************
-worker_processes 4;
+worker_processes 8;
changed: [web1]
-worker_processes 1;
+worker_processes 8;
changed: [web2]
Read another host’s variables through hostvars, for example so a web server can find the database:
ansible web1 -m ansible.builtin.debug -a "msg='{{ hostvars[\"db1\"].ansible_host }}:{{ hostvars[\"db1\"].db_port }}'"
web1 | SUCCESS =>
    msg: 192.0.2.21:5432
Read one fact:
ansible db1 -m ansible.builtin.setup -a "filter=ansible_python_version"
db1 | SUCCESS =>
    ansible_facts:
        ansible_python_version: 3.15.2

title: 6. Variables and Facts
text:
Rules and conventions

Put every knob in role defaults, with a sensible value. Override in group_vars or host_vars.
Keep -e for one-off runs and CI pipelines, not for values that belong in Git.
Define each variable in as few places as possible. Two definitions are a choice; five are a puzzle.
Use ansible_facts['name'], not the deprecated ansible_name.
Turn off facts (gather_facts: false) when no task needs them.
Check the merged result with ansible-inventory --host web1, or with a debug: var=... task.

title: 6. Variables and Facts
text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




A variable name with a dash
'lemonade' is undefined, because Jinja reads lemonade-port as subtraction.
Use underscores.


Expecting lists or dictionaries to merge
Drinks from the role default vanish.
Merge explicitly with combine, or define the full list in one place.


Setting a value in role vars/ and overriding it in group_vars
The override is ignored, because role vars are level 15.
Move it to defaults/.


Using ansible_distribution
Deprecation warning: top-level facts will not be injected after the change in 2.24.
ansible_facts['distribution'].


register inside a loop, then .stdout
object of type 'dict' has no attribute 'stdout'
Use .results[i].stdout, or loop over .results.

title: 3. Ad Hoc Commands
text:
It is a hot Saturday and the Lemonade Stand is busy. You need quick answers and quick fixes, and writing a playbook for each one would be overkill:

Which version is each web server running right now?
Put a “Closed for lunch” notice on both web servers.
Restart nginx on web2 only.

An ad hoc command runs one module on many hosts from a single line in the terminal.

title: 3. Ad Hoc Commands
text:
It is a hot Saturday and the Lemonade Stand is busy. You need quick answers and quick fixes, and writing a playbook for each one would be overkill:

Which version is each web server running right now?
Put a “Closed for lunch” notice on both web servers.
Restart nginx on web2 only.

An ad hoc command runs one module on many hosts from a single line in the terminal.

title: 3. Ad Hoc Commands
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipSimon says



In the game Simon says, one person calls out an instruction and everybody does it at once: “Simon says touch your nose!” Nobody writes anything down first. It is a single instruction, for right now.
An ad hoc command is “Simon says” for servers. ansible web -a "uptime" means “Simon says: every web server, tell me your uptime.” When you want the same instructions every week, write them into a playbook instead. That is the recipe card you keep.

title: 3. Ad Hoc Commands
text:
The concept, precisely
The shape of every ad hoc command:
ansible <pattern> -m <module> -a "<arguments>" [flags]

<pattern> chooses the hosts (lesson 2).
-m names the module. When you leave it out, Ansible uses ansible.builtin.command.
-a gives the module’s arguments, either as key=value key=value or as JSON.
Arguments are Jinja templates, so { inventory_hostname } becomes each host’s own name.

Ansible runs the module on every matched host in parallel, up to forks hosts at a time (default 5).

title: 3. Ad Hoc Commands
text:
Worked examples
All from devops/ansible/examples/. Paths in the output are shown with the default lab_root.
Which version does each web server serve?
ansible web -a "grep -o 'version .*<' {{ lab_root }}/{{ inventory_hostname }}/site/index.html"
web1 | CHANGED | rc=0 >>
version 1.1.0<
web2 | CHANGED | rc=0 >>
version 1.1.0<
CHANGED here does not mean anything changed. command cannot tell, so it always says CHANGED. rc=0 is the exit code.
A pipe needs shell. With command, ls receives |, wc and -l as file names:
ansible db1 -a "ls {{ lab_root }}/db1 | wc -l"                      # FAILED rc=1: ls: |: No such file
ansible db1 -m ansible.builtin.shell -a "ls {{ lab_root }}/db1 | wc -l"   # CHANGED rc=0 >> 2
A real module is idempotent. Run this twice:
ansible web -m ansible.builtin.copy \
  -a "content='Closed for lunch' dest={{ lab_root }}/{{ inventory_hostname }}/site/notice.txt"
web1 | CHANGED =>        # first run
    changed: true
web1 | SUCCESS =>        # second run
    changed: false
creates= makes command idempotent. It skips the command when the file already exists:
ansible db1 -a "touch {{ lab_root }}/db1/seeded creates={{ lab_root }}/db1/seeded"
db1 | CHANGED | rc=0 >>                                   # first run
db1 | SUCCESS | rc=0 >>                                   # second run
skipped, since /tmp/lemonade-lab/db1/seeded exists
On real servers, with sudo:
ansible web -b -m ansible.builtin.package -a "name=nginx state=present"
ansible web2 -b -m ansible.builtin.service -a "name=nginx state=restarted"
ansible db1 -m ansible.builtin.setup -a "filter=ansible_distribution*"

Ad hoc for questions and emergencies, playbooks for anything you repeat. If you type the same ad hoc command twice, put it in a playbook.
Look at the hosts first: add --list-hosts before any command that changes things.
Prefer a module over command/shell. Modules report changed honestly and support --check.
Quote the -a string, and use single quotes inside it.
Restarting services is not idempotent by design. state=restarted always restarts. Use state=started to only make sure a service is running.
