title: 3. Ad Hoc Commands
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
Ansible starts at most \(f\) hosts at the same time. If every host takes about the same time per task, the hosts run in waves:
\[
w = \left\lceil \frac{n}{f} \right\rceil
\]
where:

\(n\) is the number of hosts the pattern matched (a count, \(n \ge 1\));
\(f\) is the number of forks, set by -f or forks in ansible.cfg (default 5);
\(\lceil x \rceil\) (“ceiling”) rounds \(x\) up to the next whole number;
\(w\) is the number of waves.

Example. The lab has \(n = 3\) hosts.

With \(f = 5\): \(w = \lceil 3/5 \rceil = \lceil 0.6 \rceil = 1\) wave. All three run together.
With \(f = 1\): \(w = \lceil 3/1 \rceil = 3\) waves. One host at a time.

The time for one task is then roughly:
\[
T \approx w \cdot t + c
\]
where:

\(T\) is the total time in seconds;
\(t\) is the time one host needs for the task, in seconds;
\(c\) is Ansible’s fixed start-up cost, in seconds (reading the inventory, starting Python);
\(w\) is the number of waves from the formula above.

Example. In the lab, ansible all -a "sleep 1" has \(t = 1\) s. Measured on a laptop:

-f 1: \(w = 3\), so \(T \approx 3 \cdot 1 + c\). Measured: 4.3 s, which gives \(c \approx 1.3\) s.
-f 3: \(w = 1\), so \(T \approx 1 \cdot 1 + c\). Measured: 1.8 s, which gives \(c \approx 0.8\) s.

For a summer fleet of \(n = 12\) web servers with \(t = 4\) s, the default \(f = 5\) gives \(w = \lceil 12/5 \rceil = \lceil 2.4 \rceil = 3\) waves, so \(T \approx 3 \cdot 4 = 12\) s plus start-up. Raising \(f\) to 12 gives one wave, about 4 s. The formula is an approximation: real hosts take different times, and Ansible starts a new host as soon as a fork is free.

title: 4. Playbooks
4. Playbooks
4. Playbooks
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipThe team’s playbook and the pilot’s checklist



A football coach keeps a playbook. Each play says which players do what: “defenders, stay back; strikers, run left”. Ansible borrowed the name. A play says which hosts (players) run which tasks (moves).
Pilots and surgeons use checklists too. In The Checklist Manifesto (2009), the surgeon Atul Gawande tells how a simple 19-item checklist, tested in eight hospitals around the world, cut deaths after surgery from 1.5% to 0.8%. People are not bad at their jobs. They just forget steps when they are busy. A checklist never forgets.
A playbook is a checklist for computers. Computers follow it perfectly, every single time.

title: 4. Playbooks
text:
The concept, precisely

A playbook is a YAML file that holds a list of plays.
A play maps a set of hosts (hosts:) to an ordered list of tasks.
A task calls one module with arguments.
Ansible runs task by task: task 1 on all hosts, then task 2 on all hosts, and so on. This is the default linear strategy.

The first play of the lab’s site.yml:
- name: Configure the web servers   # play name, shown in the output
  hosts: web                        # which hosts (a pattern)
  gather_facts: false               # skip collecting system facts (faster)
  roles:
    - lemonade_web                  # the tasks come from this role
A play with tasks written directly in it:
- name: Configure the database server
  hosts: db
  tasks:
    - name: Write the database settings          # task name
      ansible.builtin.copy:                      # module (FQCN)
        content: "port = {{ db_port }}\n"        # module arguments
        dest: "{{ lab_root }}/db1/db.conf"

title: 4. Playbooks
text:
YAML rules that matter
Ansible files are YAML. Most beginner errors are YAML errors, not Ansible errors.









Rule
Right
Wrong
Why




Indent with spaces, never tabs
··hosts: web
⇥hosts: web
YAML forbids tabs for indentation. Two spaces is the convention.


A list item starts with -
- name: Render
-name: Render
The space after - is required.


A map entry is key: value
state: directory
state:directory
The space after : is required.


Quote a value that starts with {{
dest: "{{ path }}"
dest: {{ path }}
Unquoted { starts a YAML dictionary.


Quote a value that contains :
msg: "Price: 2.50"
msg: Price: 2.50
: would start a second key.


Write booleans as true / false
become: true
become: yes
yes, no, on, off are booleans in YAML 1.1 too, but they confuse readers. A country code NO silently becomes false.


Quote file modes
mode: "0644"
mode: 644
Unquoted 644 is the decimal number 644, which is the wrong permission. See the maths below.


\| keeps line breaks
content: \|

For files and scripts.


> folds lines into one
msg: >

For long sentences.


--- at the top is optional
---

It marks the start of a YAML document.


# starts a comment
# why we do this

Explain why, not what.

title: 4. Playbooks
text:
Reading PLAY RECAP








Counter
Meaning
Good or bad?




ok
Tasks that succeeded, including the changed ones.
Expected.


changed
Tasks that modified the host.
Expected on the first run; should be 0 on the second.


unreachable
Ansible could not connect. The host is dropped from the rest of the play.
Check SSH, DNS and the firewall.


failed
A task failed. The host stops running further tasks.
Read the error above the recap.


skipped
A when was false, or a module could not run in check mode.
Usually fine.


rescued
A failure handled by a rescue: section.
Fine. The recovery worked.


ignored
A failure hidden by ignore_errors: true.
Look at it. Something did fail.



The exit code tells scripts and CI what happened: 0 all good, 1 general error, 2 at least one host failed, 4 a host was unreachable (or the playbook could not be parsed), 5 bad command-line options, 99 you pressed Ctrl-C.

title: 4. Playbooks
text:
Rules and conventions

One playbook per purpose: site.yml builds everything; rolling-update.yml upgrades; small task files live in roles.
Name every play and task. The names are your log.
Use FQCNs: ansible.builtin.copy, not copy.
Put tasks in roles once a play has more than a handful of tasks (lesson 9).
Run --syntax-check, then --check --diff, then the real run.
Set gather_facts: false when no task uses facts. It saves one task per host.

title: 7. Jinja2 Templates
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipMad Libs



Mad Libs is a word game invented by Roger Price and Leonard Stern in the 1950s. You get a story with blanks: “Today I drank a (adjective) lemonade that cost (number) dollars.” Your friends call out words, you write them into the blanks, and you read out a funny story.
A Jinja2 template is a Mad Libs page for computers. worker_processes {{ lemonade_nginx_workers }}; has one blank. For web1 Ansible writes 4 into it; for web2 it writes 1. Templates can do one trick that Mad Libs can’t: “repeat this line for every drink on the menu”.

title: 7. Jinja2 Templates
text:
The concept, precisely

Jinja2 is a template language for Python. Ansible uses it everywhere: in playbook values, in when: conditions, and in template files.
Templating happens on the control node, before anything is sent to the host.
The ansible.builtin.template module renders a .j2 file with the host’s variables and copies the result to the host. It is copy with blanks filled in.
A filter transforms a value: { name | upper }. A test asks a yes/no question: { port is defined }. A lookup fetches data from outside, on the control node.

title: 7. Jinja2 Templates
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
Rendering a template is a function of the template text and the host’s variables:
\[
\operatorname{render}(T, V_h) = F_h
\]
where:

\(T\) is the template text, such as nginx.conf.j2;
\(V_h\) is the set of variables of host \(h\) after precedence (lesson 6);
\(F_h\) is the resulting file for host \(h\).

The same \(T\) with different \(V_h\) gives different files. That is the whole point.
Example. \(T\) = nginx.conf.j2. With \(V_{\texttt{web1}}\) containing workers = 4, \(F_{\texttt{web1}}\) has worker_processes 4;. With \(V_{\texttt{web2}}\) containing workers = 1, \(F_{\texttt{web2}}\) has worker_processes 1;.
The default filter is a piecewise function:
\[
\operatorname{default}(x, d) =
\begin{cases}
x & \text{if } x \text{ is defined} \\
d & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]
where \(x\) is the variable being read and \(d\) is the fallback value.
Example. missing | default('none'): missing is undefined, so the second case applies and the result is none. lemonade_app_port | default(80) on a web host: the variable is defined as 8080, so the first case applies and the result is 8080.
The menu total combines map and sum:
\[
P = \sum_{i=1}^{n} p_i
\]
where:

\(n\) is the number of drinks in lemonade_menu;
\(p_i\) is the price of drink \(i\), in dollars;
\(P\) is the total, which is what lemonade_menu | map(attribute='price') | sum returns.

Example. \(n = 3\), with \(p_1 = 2.50\), \(p_2 = 3.00\) and \(p_3 = 2.00\), so \(P = 2.50 + 3.00 + 2.00 = 7.50\). Ansible printed 7.5. To show it as money, use '%.2f' | format(P), which gives 7.50.
selectattr is set-builder notation:
\[
S = \lbrace\, d \in M : \operatorname{inStock}(d) \,\rbrace
\]
where \(M\) is the set of drinks on the menu, \(\operatorname{inStock}(d)\) is true when drink \(d\) has in_stock: true, and \(S\) is the drinks that pass.
Example. \(M\) = {Classic, Pink, Iced Tea}, and only Pink is out of stock, so \(S\) = {Classic, Iced Tea}. That matches the filter table above.

Every command in this book has been run from devops/ansible/examples/, and nobody typed -i inventory.yml. Why? Because a file called ansible.cfg sits in that folder and says where the inventory is.

title: 12. Configuration and Tooling
text:
Every command in this book has been run from devops/ansible/examples/, and nobody typed -i inventory.yml. Why? Because a file called ansible.cfg sits in that folder and says where the inventory is.
On a team this matters even more. If Alice has forks = 50 in her home folder and Bob has the default 5, the same playbook behaves differently for each of them. You want one project config in Git, and you want to know which settings are actually in force.

title: 12. Configuration and Tooling
text:
Explain it like I’m ten






TipThe rule book on the top of the pile



Imagine several board-game rule books stacked in a pile: one from the game box, one your family wrote, and one your class made. The house rule is simple: read only the book on the top of the pile, and ignore the others completely. You never mix page 3 from one book with page 5 from another.
Ansible looks for ansible.cfg in the same way. It checks a fixed list of places, uses the first file it finds, and ignores the rest.
There is also a referee. Whatever the rule book says, if the referee calls out a rule during the game (“this round, everyone gets two turns!”), the referee wins. Environment variables and command-line flags are the referee.

title: 12. Configuration and Tooling
text:
Where ansible.cfg is found
Ansible checks these places in order and uses the first one that exists:








Order
Location
Rule / convention




1
The file named in the ANSIBLE_CONFIG environment variable
For CI, or to test another config.


2
./ansible.cfg in the current folder
The usual choice: one per project, in Git.


3
~/.ansible.cfg in your home folder
Personal defaults. Keep it small.


4
/etc/ansible/ansible.cfg
System-wide, often installed by a package manager.



The files are not merged. If ./ansible.cfg exists, ~/.ansible.cfg is ignored completely.
The world-writable caveat. If the current folder can be written by every user (mode 777), Ansible refuses to read ./ansible.cfg from it. Another user could otherwise plant a config that runs their code. Real output:
[WARNING]: Ansible is being run in a world writable directory (.../ww), ignoring it as an ansible.cfg source.
  config file = None
Fix it with chmod 755 ., or point ANSIBLE_CONFIG at the file explicitly.

text:
Worked example
From devops/ansible/examples/, see where every non-default setting came from:
ANSIBLE_FORKS=10 ansible-config dump --only-changed
CONFIG_FILE() = <lab>/ansible.cfg
DEFAULT_FORKS(env: ANSIBLE_FORKS) = 10

title: 12. Configuration and Tooling
text:
Rules and conventions

One ansible.cfg per project, in Git, next to the playbooks. Then everyone runs with the same settings.
Keep ~/.ansible.cfg minimal. It is ignored whenever a project file is found, so anything you rely on there silently disappears inside projects.
Leave host_key_checking = True for real servers. Turning it off hides man-in-the-middle attacks.
Turn on pipelining once sudo works without requiretty. It cuts SSH round trips.
Run ansible --version when confused. The config file = line says which file won.
Run ansible-lint and --syntax-check in CI (CI/CD part).

text:
Common mistakes








Mistake
Symptom
Fix




Running from another folder
No inventory was parsed; roles not found.
cd into the project, or set ANSIBLE_CONFIG.


Expecting settings from two files to merge
A setting in ~/.ansible.cfg “does nothing”.

chmod 755 .

ansible-config validate -t all.

title: 12. Configuration and Tooling
text:
Mathematical Abstraction
Which config file. Let \(L = (\ell_1, \ell_2, \ell_3, \ell_4)\) be the list of locations above, in order. Ansible uses
\[
\operatorname{cfg} = \ell_{k}, \qquad k = \min \lbrace\, i : \ell_i \text{ exists and is allowed} \,\rbrace
\]
where:

\(\ell_1\) is the path in ANSIBLE_CONFIG, \(\ell_2\) is ./ansible.cfg, \(\ell_3\) is ~/.ansible.cfg, and \(\ell_4\) is /etc/ansible/ansible.cfg;
“allowed” excludes \(\ell_2\) when the current folder is world-writable;
\(\min\) picks the smallest index \(i\) that qualifies, so \(k\) is the position of the first usable file;
if no location qualifies, there is no config file and every setting has its default.

Example 1, the lab: ANSIBLE_CONFIG is not set, so \(\ell_1\) does not exist. ./ansible.cfg exists and the folder is not world-writable, so the set contains 2 (and maybe 3 and 4), and \(k = 2\). The lab file wins. ansible --version confirms it on its config file = line.
Example 2, the same folder after chmod 777 .: \(\ell_2\) is no longer allowed. If neither \(\ell_3\) nor \(\ell_4\) exists, the set is empty, and the real output above shows config file = None.
Which value for one setting. For a setting \(x\), each layer \(j\) may give a value \(v_j(x)\):
\[
\operatorname{value}(x) = v_{j^\ast}(x), \qquad j^\ast = \max \lbrace\, j : v_j(x) \text{ is set} \,\rbrace
\]
where:

\(j \in \lbrace 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 \rbrace\) numbers the layers config file, environment, command line, playbook keyword and variable, from weakest to strongest;
\(v_j(x)\) is the value that layer \(j\) gives, if any;
\(j^\ast\) is the strongest layer that sets \(x\).

Example, forks: ansible.cfg says forks = 5 (\(v_1 = 5\)), the environment has ANSIBLE_FORKS=10 (\(v_2 = 10\)), and the command has -f 20 (\(v_3 = 20\)). Then \(j^\ast = \max \lbrace 1, 2, 3 \rbrace = 3\), so Ansible uses 20 forks. Remove -f 20 and \(j^\ast = 2\): 10, which is what dump --only-changed printed. With lesson 3’s wave formula, 12 hosts then need \(\lceil 12/10 \rceil = 2\) waves instead of \(\lceil 12/5 \rceil = 3\).

This book teaches the tools that take a small web application from a laptop to servers that stay up:

Every chapter uses the same tiny business, so you never have to learn a new scenario.

The Lemonade Stand is a web page that shows a lemonade menu and its prices. Customers open it in a browser. The owner wants it to stay online, to change prices without breaking anything, and to add new drinks every week.

The parts


Part 1: Ansible
Inventories, ad-hoc commands, playbooks, modules, variables and facts, Jinja2 templates, loops and handlers, roles, Vault and rolling deployments. The lab pretends your laptop is three servers.

title: DevOps: A Hands-On Book
text:
Why k3s instead of “full” Kubernetes
Kubernetes is powerful, but a production installation has many separate pieces to install, secure and upgrade. k3s is a CNCF-certified Kubernetes distribution packaged as one binary. It bundles a container runtime, networking, DNS, an ingress controller, a load balancer and local storage. It is the same Kubernetes API, so every manifest and kubectl command in Part 2 also works on a large cluster later. You just have much less to set up while you learn.

title: DevOps: A Hands-On Book
section: How to read the math in this book
text:
How to read the math in this book
The mathematics here is small. It turns a rule into one exact line, such as “how many batches will a rolling update take?”. Every lesson defines its symbols again where they are used, but this table collects them in one place.









Symbol
Read it as
Meaning
Example




\(x \in S\)
“\(x\) is in \(S\)”
\(x\) is a member of the set \(S\)
\(\texttt{web1} \in \lbrace \texttt{web1}, \texttt{web2} \rbrace\)


\(x \notin S\)
“\(x\) is not in \(S\)”
\(x\) is not a member of \(S\)
\(\texttt{db1} \notin \lbrace \texttt{web1}, \texttt{web2} \rbrace\)


\(A \cup B\)
“\(A\) union \(B\)”
everything in \(A\) or \(B\)
\(\lbrace 1, 2 \rbrace \cup \lbrace 2, 3 \rbrace = \lbrace 1, 2, 3 \rbrace\)


\(A \cap B\)
“\(A\) intersect \(B\)”
only what is in both \(A\) and \(B\)
\(\lbrace 1, 2 \rbrace \cap \lbrace 2, 3 \rbrace = \lbrace 2 \rbrace\)


\(A \setminus B\)
“\(A\) minus \(B\)”
what is in \(A\) but not in \(B\)
\(\lbrace 1, 2 \rbrace \setminus \lbrace 2, 3 \rbrace = \lbrace 1 \rbrace\)


\(A \subseteq B\)
“\(A\) is a subset of \(B\)”
every member of \(A\) is also in \(B\)
\(\lbrace 1 \rbrace \subseteq \lbrace 1, 2 \rbrace\)


\(\lvert S \rvert\)
“size of \(S\)”
how many members \(S\) has
\(\lvert \lbrace \texttt{web1}, \texttt{web2}, \texttt{db1} \rbrace \rvert = 3\)


\(\emptyset\)
“the empty set”
a set with no members
\(\lbrace 1 \rbrace \cap \lbrace 2 \rbrace = \emptyset\)


\(\lceil x \rceil\)
“ceiling of \(x\)”
the smallest whole number \(\ge x\) (round up)
\(\lceil 2.5 \rceil = 3\), \(\lceil 3 \rceil = 3\)


\(\lfloor x \rfloor\)
“floor of \(x\)”
the largest whole number \(\le x\) (round down)
\(\lfloor 2.5 \rfloor = 2\)


\(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i\)
“sum of \(a_i\) for \(i\) from 1 to \(n\)”
\(a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_n\)
\(\sum_{i=1}^{3} i = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6\)


\(x^n\)
“\(x\) to the power \(n\)”
\(x\) multiplied by itself \(n\) times
\(2^{8} = 256\)


\(\max(a, b)\)
“maximum of \(a\) and \(b\)”
the larger value
\(\max(4, 7) = 7\)


\(\min(a, b)\)
“minimum of \(a\) and \(b\)”
the smaller value
\(\min(4, 7) = 4\)


\(f(x)\)
“\(f\) of \(x\)”
apply the rule \(f\) to the input \(x\)
if \(f(x) = 2x\) then \(f(3) = 6\)


\(f(f(s)) = f(s)\)
“doing it twice equals doing it once”
idempotent: repeating the action changes nothing more
“make sure the light is on”, done twice, leaves it on


\(P \Rightarrow Q\)
“if \(P\) then \(Q\)”
whenever \(P\) is true, \(Q\) must be true
“a test fails” \(\Rightarrow\) “the deploy stops”


\(P \land Q\)
“\(P\) and \(Q\)”
both are true
two conditions in an Ansible when: list


\(P \lor Q\)
“\(P\) or \(Q\)”
at least one is true
web:db selects hosts in web or db


\(\neg P\)
“not \(P\)”
\(P\) is false
!db excludes the db group


\(a \le b\)
“\(a\) is at most \(b\)”
\(a\) is smaller than or equal to \(b\)
requested CPU \(\le\) available CPU


\(\approx\)
“is about”
an approximate value
\(1/3 \approx 0.33\)



A worked example combines several of these symbols. Ansible runs a task on at most \(f\) hosts at a time. With \(n\) hosts it therefore needs
\[
w = \left\lceil \frac{n}{f} \right\rceil
\]
where:

\(w\) is the number of waves (rounds) needed, a whole number;
\(n\) is the number of target hosts;
\(f\) is the forks setting, the largest number of hosts Ansible works on at once;
\(\lceil \cdot \rceil\) rounds the division up, because a half-full wave still takes a whole round.

Example: the Lemonade fleet has \(n = 3\) hosts. With the default \(f = 5\), \(w = \lceil 3/5 \rceil = \lceil 0.6 \rceil = 1\) wave. With \(f = 2\), \(w = \lceil 3/2 \rceil = \lceil 1.5 \rceil = 2\) waves: web1 and web2 first, then db1.
